title: How a small consultancy should write an about page
metaTitle: How a small consultancy writes an about page
excerpt: Name who will be in the working session and what they will refuse. Keep an origin story only if it changes the decision to book.
alt: A laptop open to a code editor on a white desk, beside a plant and a yellow mug, a working desk rather than a founding myth.
caption: The page should show the person at the work, not the origin story. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What belongs in the first line of a consultant's bio?
faqs.answer: Name the problem they take, in the words a buyer uses when they complain. Follow with the verbs of the session: force the decision, write the notes, refuse a second problem. A line about passion does not tell the buyer who will stop them postponing.

faqs.question: When should the founding story stay?
faqs.answer: Keep a short origin paragraph only when it predicts the session, such as a refusal to end without a decision someone else can use. A leap-of-faith founding year does not change the booking. If you delete the story and the bios still hold, the story was atmosphere.

faqs.question: What should the about page ask the visitor to do?
faqs.answer: Ask them to book a session with the person who takes that problem. If you assign the person after they book, say so in a sentence you can keep. Do not put a newsletter button at the same weight as the booking.

sources.title: Influencing your title links in search results

markdown:
A small consultancy about page is proof that a specific person will sit in the working session. Name who does the work, and why a buyer comparing you with doing it themselves should care. Skip the origin myth unless it changes their decision to book. Google's helpful-content guidance treats "who" as part of trust: it should be evident who is responsible, and background should be available where a reader would expect it. A page that never names a person fails that test.

The buyer is not choosing a legend. They are choosing who will be across the table when they try to postpone the decision again. Write for that hour. If they could run the session themselves, your bio has to show why they have not.

## Name the person who will be in the room

Start with the people who take the sessions, not with a founding year. For each person, four facts. Their name. The problem they actually take. What they do in the session, in verbs: force the decision, write the notes, refuse the second problem. What they do not do. A researcher should not be introduced as the principal if they will not be the one who says the recommendation out loud.

Keep the bios short enough to compare. A buyer with one stuck problem wants the one or two people who take that problem, not a directory. If the firm is one person, say so. A single clear bio is better than a "collective" with no names. An unnamed collective is how a DIY buyer decides they would rather keep the work, because at least they know who will do it.

Put the problem in the first line. "Takes pricing decisions for founder-led product companies that still quote in a spreadsheet." A buyer can match that to their complaint. "Passionate about helping leaders" matches every firm they have already decided not to hire.

If someone is leaving, or only prepares materials, do not present them as the person in the room. The page is a promise of presence. Update it when the roster changes. An outdated name is a small lie, and this buyer is comparing you with their own reliability.

## Why they should care, which is the problem

The second sentence is the reason, and the reason is the decision, not the personality. "She will not leave the room with six priorities" is a reason. "He loves trail running" is a life. The life can sit at the end if you want the firm to sound human. It cannot be the reason to book.

Write the reason as a constraint the buyer recognizes in themselves. You require the person who can say yes to attend. You will stop the session if the artifact they promised to bring is not there. You have sat on their side of this problem, if that is true, and you say in what kind of company. Do not borrow a biography. A fabricated "operator" is worse than a plain description of someone who is good at forcing a decision.

Google also asks whether the content shows first-hand experience. On this page, first-hand means the problems they have actually taken, described specifically enough to check. "Fifteen years advising companies" is a duration. "Pricing sessions with founder-led firms that leave with a list they can send" is experience. Only write the second if it is true. A round number you cannot define is the kind of claim this buyer uses as a reason to do it themselves.

Skip awards unless the buyer would know the award and it changes the booking. A badge wall decorates an about page when the bios do not yet say the problem.

## When an origin story earns a paragraph

An origin story earns its place when it predicts the session. The firm was started by someone who kept rewriting quotes at midnight and now refuses to end a session without a price someone else can send. That sentence can stay. The firm was started after a leap of faith. That sentence can go. It does not change the booking.

Use the delete test. Remove the origin paragraph. Read the page to someone who has the problem. If they would still book, the paragraph was atmosphere. If they are newly unsure who will be in the room, you deleted a bio, or you never wrote one.

Keep the founder's story in the founder's voice only if they still take the sessions. A firm that has grown past the founder should lead with the people in current rooms. The founder can have a bio in the same format, with the same demand: the problem, the verbs, a true constraint.

One sentence of history is enough if you want one, and it should attach to a refusal. "We have taken this problem since we started, and we still decline it when the decision-maker will not attend." History in service of a boundary is useful. History as mood is how a tasteful interior sneaks back in as prose.

## What does not belong in the bio

Cut lines that could move onto another firm's site unchanged. "Trusted advisor." "Thought partner." "Passionate about impact." A buyer who might do the work themselves has read these and gone back to their own document. The words do not predict the hour.

Cut the client logo row unless you can say the problem and the decision. A logo without a decision is borrowed reputation. If you can name the constraint, it belongs on a proof page. The about page can point to it in one sentence. Do not make this page a second, vaguer case-study wall.

Cut hobbies if they push the problem below the first screen on a phone. The first screen should still answer who takes the problem the homepage named. A dog can wait. If it cannot, the page is being written for the team.

Titles need the same honesty. Google's guidance on title links warns against vague labels such as "Profile," and against boilerplate that makes every page sound alike. "About" is a vague label. "Who is in the pricing session" describes the page. Give each person a heading with their name and the problem. Do not give "Our story" the same size as the name of the person who will take the booking.

## A page they will still sign

The people on the page should read their block without wincing. Read the constraint aloud. If they say they would not actually refuse that, take it out. An about page that overclaims becomes an argument in the session, when the buyer quotes you and you soften it.

Agree on a revision rule. Bios change when the problem they take changes, not when someone wants a fresher adjective. A quarterly pass is enough if the work is stable. The day a principal leaves is not optional. The buyer who books from a bio of a person who is gone will treat every later sentence as decoration, and they will be right.

Keep a private note of sentences you refused to publish. It helps the next time a new joiner wants to sound more senior than the problems they take. The page is a roster of present work.

## How the page hands them the session

The about page should not re-explain the fee or list every offer. It has one exit: book a session with the person who takes that problem, or with the problem if you assign the person after they book. If you assign after, say so. "You will meet the person who will run the session, not a coordinator who will hand you off." If you cannot promise it, do not write it.

A line under the bios can say what to bring. The postponed decision. The person who can say yes. The draft they are embarrassed by. You are not asking for a briefing book. You are asking for enough to know the session is real.

Do not put a second exit of equal weight beside the booking. A newsletter button next to the session splits the page. The about page is for the buyer deciding whether this person is safer than another month alone.

Read each bio without the name. If a colleague cannot tell who it is, the bio is still a template. Add the problem and the verb until the paragraph could only belong to that person. Then read the page to someone who has been doing the work themselves. Ask who would be in the room, and what that person would refuse. If either answer is fuzzy, the page is still an origin story with a portrait.

When the bios can carry a real problem, the next piece is a decision, not another adjective. Read [how a proof page should show the constraint they would have delayed](/blog/proof-pages-for-a-small-consultancy) before you paste logos under the bios and call it evidence.

If you want to pressure-test whether a bio would make you book, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the paragraph you are willing to put under your own name.
